tools.title: The NYT/Siena polls show a blue tsunami
tools.summary_raw: They might be wrong again, but it’s getting hard to deny that polls point toward a really big year for Democrats.
tools.content_text: Getty Images I woke up very early today. 1 Believe it or not, I get more sleep than you might assume — and the extra hour helped — but I’m no longer as much of a night owl as I pretend to be. One thing I’ve always had trouble doing, though, is sleeping when I have some sort of non-negotiable commitment in the morning. Like, if I have to wake up at 6 a.m. to catch an 8 a.m. flight at LaGuardia 2 , my body clock might wake me up at 4:45 instead. Maybe it was because I was anticipating a new round of New York Times/Siena University polls, which are sometimes published at 5 a.m. The morning turned into an anticlimax , without much new data. But NYT/Siena released their presumably final set of polls this evening, and they showed what can only be described as fantastic numbers for Democrats, putting them ahead — sometimes narrowly, sometimes not — in basically every Senate battleground and in the associated governor’s races, including in Texas: These polls weren’t quite in the territory of FLIPR’s officially “weird” scenarios , but they're close to that boundary. Even if Democrats were to lose a couple of these races — and there’s actually some bad news for them here in Alaska, I think — absolutely no Democrat is going to complain if they only flip the top five races in this chart, especially if it comes along with the Texas governorship. The Times/Siena polls are also not that surprising, given that the NYT shows a D +11 on the generic ballot and that, in most cases, the trends in their polls follow the patterns FLIPR has previously detected . Although the model trusts the NYT/Siena polls a lot — they’re among our more highly-rated pollsters — it does adjust every survey firm’s numbers for house effects . In other words, it knows that NYT/Siena has tended to have good numbers for Democrats this cycle, and that’s priced into its forecasts, including to some extent even in races that the NYT hasn’t polled. We’ve left the ambiguous zone The other reason I didn’t sleep so soundly last night, I’ll admit, is because I have a fair bit of anxiety about the election. In the Senate, FLIPR has sort of been teetering on the boundary between a “Lean D” and a “Likely D” forecast — formally, this is defined as a 75 percent chance of winning — in a way that felt slightly uncomfortable. I don’t want to get too “meta” here — there’s been enough of that in the newsletter — but we were sort of in an ambiguous place where it wasn’t quite clear whether pollsters and modelers should “own” the fact that they were projecting a big night for Democrats — and own the risk of another embarrassing systematic polling error . The NYT/Siena polls resolve that, in my opinion, in Democrats’ favor, for better or worse. Polls show that Democrats will win the Senate, perhaps soundly. They might be wrong or they might predict slightly the wrong states to flip. No currently R-held state other than North Carolina counts as “Solid D”. […]

tools.title: Could Haley Stevens cost Democrats the Senate?
tools.summary_raw: Probably not, but let’s run the numbers on a rare *November* Surprise. Plus, please join us for our Election Night coverage!
tools.content_text: U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens at a primary night watch party on Aug. 4 in Detroit. She narrowly lost later that night to Abdul El-Sayed. Finn Gomez/Getty Images. With 48 hours to go until votes begin to be counted on Tuesday night, I don’t really have time for anything other than full transparency. We’d planned to probably publish a second post today — please see our fun morning post with 13 quasi-randomly selected FLIPR maps — and this second post was originally slotted in as a relatively naked advertisement for our Election Night coverage, which we’ll be co-hosting with the good folks at The Argument , GD Politics and Slow Boring . If everything goes to plan, we’ll have both a (free) live video stream and a paid-subscribers-only liveblog. 1 I’m mostly going to be focused on the liveblog component, but we’ll have plenty of insightful contributors for you on both channels. Subscribe now I figured the post would start by talking about some of Sunday morning’s more interesting polls. But surprise #1: there weren’t many polls , nor were any of them all that interesting. Incentives in the industry are changing, and not necessarily in a good way. Sundays used to be big days for politics coverage back in the era of Sunday newspaper print editions and when shows like Meet the Press were incredibly influential. Now, the conventional wisdom seems to be that you fire out your best stuff on weekdays instead. 2 Plus, high-quality polling is expensive, and pollsters may feel like they’re in a no-win position where they’ll either get accused of herding or risk publishing an outlier-ish poll that will surely get them criticized if they’re wrong — or who knows, maybe even sued by the president ? But then early this afternoon, we got a real surprise: Haley Stevens, whom Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the August Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, endorsed his Republican opponent Mike Rogers . I’m going to be honest that I thought this was a fake headline when I first came across it on Twitter, sort of like I originally worried I might be hallucinating when I first heard about the Luka Doncic trade . 3 I’m also going to be honest that I’ve sort of tuned out stories about the Democratic infighting in Michigan. Don’t get me wrong: we love talking about Democratic infighting at Silver Bulletin, love it, love it, love it . But it’s pretty much the only thing that anyone is going to be talking about in politics from early next year onward, when candidates begin to declare for the 2028 race, until the DNC in Boston, Denver, or Philadelphia in August 2028. You can watch the Stevens video for yourself, but to me at least, she comes across as fairly petty and vindictive. To be fair, though, so has El-Sayed , who disinvited Stevens from campaign events. There’s not much maturity on display here. If Democrats had to do it over again, maybe they’d have nominated Mallory McMorrow, or begged Gary Peters to run for another term. […]

tools.title: 13 maps for the morning after the midterms
tools.summary_raw: From the base case to the increasingly weird, let’s let FLIPR have some fun. 🐬
tools.content_text: At FiveThirtyEight, we sometimes experimented with showing readers a randomly selected cross-section of our election simulations to demonstrate how our models worked. I’m not sure that quite had the desired effect. Our customers tended to scroll through the simulations until they’d encounter one of the weirder maps , and then they’d sometimes use that as a way to express doubt about the forecast. But weird things happen in elections. Barack Obama improbably 1 won Indiana in 2008, and then the Hoosier State reverted back to basically where it had always been. On other occasions, results that seemed weird at the time made more sense in retrospect. Amidst a blue wave, Democratic Senator Bill Nelson lost in Florida in 2018, a state which at the time was only slightly to the right of the electoral tipping point. (Hillary Clinton had barely lost Florida in 2016.) That was the canary in the coal mine for a death spiral for Democrats in Florida . Still, let’s give the “show me the maps!” concept one more spin. This time, we’ll curate things a bit more. 2 From among the 40,000 simulations that FLIPR ran on Saturday, I’ve chosen 13 scenarios: nine or ten relatively normal cases, and then three or four deliberately weird ones. To be fair, that distinction can get blurry. We’ll show you one map where Republicans hold the House as well as the Senate , something that’s rather unlikely if you believe FLIPR. In 2024, literally the exact most frequently-occurring map from our simulations “hit”, which involved Donald Trump winning precisely the seven canonical swing states that year but nothing beyond those. Often, however, maps are messier than people expect, especially in midterms. But I’ll try to give you a representative flavor of the sorts of simulations FLIPR is cooking up. Not all of these are necessarily equally likely, however. They will include nine maps where Democrats flip the Senate and four where they don’t. That ratio is just slightly off from FLIPR’s roughly 3-to-1 odds for Democrats in the Senate, but close enough. There are lots of maps along the lines of “Democrats win 51 Senate seats, not including Texas” and “Democrats win 52 Senate seats, because James Talarico just gets barely over the finish line in Texas.” Still, in curating these, I can’t get the Anna Karenina principle out of my head: “all happy families are alike [but] each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.” The maps where FLIPR kind of breaks — either there’s a Democratic mega-tsunami, or a polling bust — are more interesting than the ones where the model’s predictions are basically about right. There’s also another point that I’ll try to layer in here. As much as we hope you’ll join us for our Election Night coverage, there’s a reasonably good chance that the midterm outcome, especially in the Senate, won’t be clear by Tuesday night or early Wednesday morning.
